paras: The killing of Knowles by an Atlanta bailiff took place in Atlanta, Georgia, in about August 1903, when J. F. Wood, a justice court bailiff, went with a money lender to a Black family's house to collect a small debt and shot and killed the husband of the woman who owed it. Wood and the lender were indicted for murder in September, and Wood was later acquitted by a jury that deliberated about twenty minutes. The Cleveland Gazette reprinted the case under the headline "Deliberately Murdered" as an example of "Georgia justice."

The debt was owed to a money lender named "Mr. Brockman" in the trial testimony reprinted by the Gazette and "J. W. Brockinon" in an Atlanta dispatch to the Savannah Morning News. According to Mrs. Knowles, the amount was 90 cents, and the bailiff and the lender told her they had a warrant for her for it. The two sources name the dead man differently: the Gazette's text, drawn from the Atlanta Constitution's trial report, calls him Knowles, while the Savannah dispatch calls him "Bob Noland, a negro."

Mrs. Knowles testified that when the two men came to her house she sent for her husband, who offered to settle the debt. In her account the bailiff refused to talk with him and shot at him, and he ran from the house; one of the four shots fired killed him. Three Black witnesses, Mabel Lovejoy, Robert Todd and Buber Jones, swore that they saw the shooting and gave practically the same account.

Wood gave a different version, stating that the man was throwing bricks at him when he fired and that he feared for his life. The Savannah dispatch described the encounter only as a dispute "in which the negro was killed."

On September 11, 1903, a grand jury in Atlanta indicted Wood and Brockinon on the charge of murder. At Wood's trial the defense put no witnesses on the stand and relied on his own statement, which his attorneys dwelt on. The case went to the jury at about 4:40, and a verdict acquitting Wood of murder was read about twenty minutes later. The coverage does not show whether Brockinon, indicted with Wood, was tried.

On November 11 the Fulton County grand jury, in a campaign against usury, returned misdemeanor true bills against Wood, two other bailiffs and two money lenders, in a dispatch that did not mention the killing.

The white coverage found consists of two short Atlanta dispatches in the Savannah Morning News. The first, headed "Bailiff and Loan Man Indicted for Murder," reported the indictment in a few sentences, identified the victim as "a negro" and gave neither the witnesses' nor Wood's version of the shooting. The second, headed "In War Against Usury," named Wood among bailiffs and lenders charged with misdemeanors and made no reference to the death. The Atlanta Constitution's report of the trial, which the reprinted text names as its source, does not appear in the coverage.

The Cleveland Gazette ran the story on its front page on November 14, 1903, under the headline "Deliberately Murdered. The Way It Is Done Down in Georgia—One of Many Cases," crediting it to the "S. W. Christian Advocate." That text called the lender a "money shark" and judged the verdict "a sample of Georgia justice, and in the capital city at that," noting that Wood felt so sure of acquittal that he presented no witnesses. It added that his word was "worth that of many Negroes" and warned that "where a Negro's life is held so cheap it will yet be found that a white man's is not worth much."

The circumstances of the shooting rest on two versions given at the trial: Mrs. Knowles and three witnesses said the bailiff refused to talk and fired as her husband offered to pay, while Wood said he fired because the man was throwing bricks at him. The sources also differ on the victim's name, Knowles or Bob Noland, and on the lender's, Brockman or Brockinon, differences the coverage does not resolve.

reader.title: Killing of Knowles by an Atlanta bailiff
bases: A justice court bailiff, J. F. Wood, serving a debt warrant with a money lender, shot and killed a Black man and was indicted and tried for murder (A1, A3, A4).

A Savannah Morning News Atlanta dispatch (A1) and the Atlanta Constitution trial report reprinted in the Cleveland Gazette (A3, A4) independently agree that bailiff J. F. Wood, collecting a money lender's debt, killed a Black man in Atlanta; they differ on the victim's name and the circumstances of the shooting.
